analytic.title: ATLAS: Aging-Aware Task Replication for Multicore Safety-Critical Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A major requirement of safety-critical systems is high reliability at low power consumption. Dynamic voltage and frequency (v/f) scaling (DVFS) techniques are widely exploited to reduce power consumption. However, DVFS through downscaling v/f levels has a negative impact on the reliability of the tasks running on the cores, and through upscaling v/f levels has circuitlevel aging effects. To achieve high reliability in multicore safetycritical systems, task replication as a fault-tolerant technique is an established way to deal with the negative effect of downscaling v/f levels, but it may accelerate aging effects due to elevating the on-chip temperatures. In this paper, we propose an aging-aware task replication (called ATLAS) method that solves the problem of satisfying the desired reliability target for a set of periodic hard real-time tasks which are executed on a multicore system. The proposed method satisfies the reliability target of the tasks through updating the required number of replicas for each task at different years. We replicate the tasks through our proposed formulas such that the reliability target is satisfied. However, task replication increases the temperature of the system and accelerates aging. To decelerate aging, we attempt to reduce the temperature while mapping and scheduling the tasks. We have also developed a modified demand bound function (DBF) for our aging-aware task replication method to verify scheduling the realtime tasks. Compared to the existing state-of-the-art techniques, experimental results for safety-critical applications on different configurations of multicore systems demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed method. Experiments show that our proposed method improves schedulability on average by 16.1% and reduces the temperature on average by 7.4 • C compared to state-of-the-art methods while meeting the system reliability target.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The non-ideal technology scaling and extensive density of integration lead to increased power consumption and high temperature, which in turn accelerate the aging and degrade the reliability of multicore systems [1]- [3]. The emergence of advanced multicore platforms into safety-critical systems provides a natural opportunity for implementing fault-tolerant techniques to achieve high reliability. However, using established fault-tolerant techniques to tackle a particular reliability concern [4] (e.g., soft errors) may lead to other reliability concerns, such as accelerated aging [5]. Moreover, certain fault-tolerant techniques (such as [6]) may lead to elevating 1 Fig. 1: Frequency reduction of a processing core and increase of average execution time of a task at different technology nodes at different years due to aging. on-chip temperatures, which further jeopardizes the reliability through aging effects, e.g., Electromigration and Negative Bias Temperature Instability (NBTI) [2], leading to permanent failure of processing cores.

To avoid temperature increases beyond the safe operating limits, Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) technique is employed on the chip to throttle down the frequency of the processing cores [3], [6]. However, this may lead to the violation of the hard timing constraints of the executing tasks, which is not acceptable for safety-critical systems [6]. Therefore, system-level techniques enforce temperature constraints on the chip while avoiding missing tasks' deadlines [6]. The DVFS techniques can further impact the reliability of the tasks through the increased fault rate due to the higher temporal vulnerability and dependence of soft error rates on lower operating voltages. On the other hand, aging mechanisms have negative effects on the operating frequency of the processing cores. Since the operating frequency depends on the aging mechanisms, designers of safety-critical systems should find its impact on reliability. As seen in Fig. 1, when the technology node advances, frequency degradation becomes worse and worse. In this figure, we have considered the aging effect due to NBTI. When the gate is negatively biased, NBTI is an important aging mechanism that affects PMOS transistors [2], [3]. NBTI inducts positive charge accumulation at the oxide-substrate interface and in the oxide layer, and hence, it increases the threshold voltage [7] [8]- [10]. As a result, the circuit-level delay increases, and the system-level frequency decreases, leading to degrading reliability. Moreover, the average execution time of a task (Dijkstra from the MiBench benchmark suite [11]) increases and some deadlines can be missed (key observation 1 ). It should be noted that we construct Fig. 1 based on the model presented in Section II.B and consider ARM Cortex-A15 at different years. Consequently, since multicore safety-critical systems should meet the timing, temperature, and reliability constraints, considering aging for these systems will be a complex problem. This is because by considering aging effects, we will face new challenges and thereby we should completely change mapping and scheduling the tasks on the system. The safety-critical systems should guarantee all the constraints in the worst-case scenario in the design time because they are used in critical applications such as medical [12]. In safety-critical systems, all timing constraints should be guaranteed in the design time (i.e., offline), before putting the system in operation (i.e., runtime) [12]. If some tasks do not meet their timing constraints (because of the aging effect), the safety-critical system should notify this fact in advance. In Fig. 1, we have considered the worst-case scenario of running tasks on the mentioned processing core. To do this, we consider the utilization of the cores to be full and all the parameters of aging to be worst. We must do this because in safety-critical systems the average-case scenario is not a suitable case for analyzing these systems [12]. Moreover, Fig. 1 is a motivational example for showing the trend of the frequency reduction due to aging effects in the worst-case scenario in different technology sizes when the utilization of the system is full. As we will mention in Section II, our aging model depends on NBTI. However, the proposed method in this paper is orthogonal to NBTI and can be exploited for any aging phenomenon (see equations 1-3). We should mention that the average frequency reduction due to the aging effect in different technology sizes is 14.5% which is the common case. Actually, the worst value reduction of frequency happens in the 14nm technology (about 30%) that is because of several parameters that increase the aging effect in this technology. At run time, if the worst-case does not happen, we exploit the actual reduction of the frequency for increasing the reliability and reducing the temperature of the system to increase the lifetime of the system. In Fig. 1, the aging effect is in the worst-case Temperature and stress phase. Also, the constant parameters and the details of different technology sizes for constructing Fig. 1 are shown in Table I.

To show the motivation of this work, in Fig. 2, we calculate the required number of replicas (see subsection II.C) for two selected tasks (Susan and Dijkstra) from the MiBench benchmark suite [11] to satisfy a specified task-level reliability target (equal to 1 -10 -7 which is the level B from the standard DO-178B [41]) running on ARM Cortex-A15 at different years. In this motivation, we have considered that Fig. 2: Motivational example of the required number of replicas for two tasks selected from MiBench [11] under aging mechanism running on ARM Cortex-A15 at different years. the variation of the frequency is computed based on Fig. 1 in 14nm. This figure shows that to satisfy the reliability target, we should employ a new task replication mechanism and update the number of replicas according to the reliability at different years. As shown in Fig. 2, at the start time of the system, Susan and Dijkstra require one replica, while after passing 5 years, they need more replicas. It should be noted that, to the best of our knowledge, none of the previous works in safety-critical systems consider aging-aware task replication. However, adding more replicas will increase the temperature on the chip and might increase beyond safe limits. As shown in Fig. 3, when the number of replicas increases after a few years, the maximum temperature of the chip increases up to 63.9 • C (key observation 2 ) which violates the temperature threshold (i.e., 60 • C). To prevent thermal violations, it is necessary to consider a temperature threshold. Note that none of the previous work in the context of safety-critical systems considered the aging-aware task replication method such that the reliability, timing, and temperature constraint are met. We have discussed the related work in Section VI and shown their limitations. The goal of this paper is to present a method that meets reliability, temperature, and timing constraints under aging effects.

div.head: A. Our Novel Contribution
div.p: In this work, the required number of replicas is determined to satisfy the task-level reliability target at different years. Indeed, the required number of replicas is computed based on the aging effect. To meet the temperature constraint, the voltage and frequency level of each task set before executing the tasks. To cope with this challenge, a temperature threshold as the Thermal Safe Power (TSP) constraint is exploited [13]. TSP is "an abstraction that provides thermally safe power constraint as a function of the number of simultaneously active cores" [13]. If the power consumption of each core is below TSP, thermal violations are avoided. Then, the tasks are replicated such that the reliability target is satisfied. To manage the aging effects, in each hyperperiod, the tasks based on their peak power consumption are sorted in ascending order. Then, the tasks are mapped to the cores based on the lowest temperature policy such that the utilization constraints of all cores are met. Note that in the lowest temperature policy, a core with the minimum value of temperature on the chip is selected to execute the task, and then the temperature of all cores is updated. After mapping the tasks to the cores, the tasks and their replicas should be scheduled on the cores based on and scheduling policy. In this paper, the partitioned Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling policy is employed. The EDF scheduling policy is a well-established scheduling algorithm exploited in safety-critical systems to schedule hard real-time periodic tasks. This scheduling algorithm considers dynamic priority assignments for the tasks. During scheduling the tasks, whenever a scheduling event occurs (e.g., a task finishes or a new task arrives) a task with the earliest deadline is selected to be scheduled on the designated core. In order to check the schedulability of the task set on the system, a unified demand bound function (DBF) analysis will be developed. At runtime, since in the task replication mechanism, only at most one successful replica of each job is needed, after that each job finishes successfully, the execution of the remaining parts of its other corresponding replica job(s) are canceled to further reduce the temperature of the systems. In a nutshell, the notable contributions of this paper are:

• Proposing an aging-aware task replication for determining the exact number of replicas for each task to satisfy the system reliability target at different years. • To satisfy the task-level reliability target along with meeting the timing and temperature constraints, a temperatureaware mapping policy is proposed. • Developing an execution time-aware DBF-based schedulability test, under timing, power, and reliability constraints.

• At runtime, according to the proposed task-dropping mechanism due to successfully executing the original jobs, we remap and re-schedule the original and replica tasks to further reduce the aging effects. Fig. 4 shows the simple system diagram of our proposed method. To evaluate our proposed method, we have employed open-source and well-adopted tool chains like gem5 [14],

McPAT [15], HotSpot [16], and TSP [11]. Compared to the existing state-of-the-art techniques, experimental results for safety-critical applications on different configurations of multicore systems demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed method. Experiments show that our proposed method improves schedulability on average by 16.1% and reduces the temperature on average by 7.4 • C compared to state-of-the-art methods, while keeping the system reliability at the required level.

Organization: Section 2 explains our models and assumptions. In Section 3, the problem definition is presented. In Section 4, the details of our ATLAS method are introduced. The experimental results are discussed in Section 5. Finally, the conclusion of the paper is presented in Section 6.

div.head: II. MODELS AND PRELIMINARIES
div.p: In this section, the system, workload, aging, and reliability models are presented.

div.head: A. System and Workload Model
div.p: In this paper, a homogeneous multicore system with m cores C = {C 1 , C 2 , . . . , C m } that executes a set of n periodic hard real-time tasks ϕ = {T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T n } is considered, where the number of tasks is more than the number of cores. The total power consumption of the system consists of dynamic and static components [17], [18]. Note that the static power is dominated by the leakage current, and the dynamic power is commonly consumed due to workload activity [17], [18]. Each hard real-time task T i on this system has a worst-case execution time wc i at the maximum v/f level and a period d i . Note that the relative deadline of each job J ij is equal to the corresponding period d i . However, our proposed method works for the periodic task set when the the relative deadline of each job is less than the corresponding period. To do this, we develop a modified DBF analysis in subsection IV.B. According to the periodic model, the j th job of each task T i (J ij ) arrives at time r ij = (j -1) × d i and must complete not later than its hard deadline
div.formula: f ij = j × d i . The utilization of the task T i is defined as U i = wc i /d i .
div.p: The sum of all tasks utilization running on the system is U tot , and the utilization of each underlying core k is Ucore,k which is the sum of all assigned tasks utilization on the core k. It should be noted that each task has just one active job at any time. In addition to timing parameters, each job J ij in ϕ is assumed to have a priority to indicate how its jobs are scheduled. The priorities set based on the dynamic priority of the Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling policy.

div.head: B. Aging Model
div.p: In this paper, aging due to NBTI is considered. However, the proposed method in this paper is orthogonal to NBTI and can be exploited for any aging phenomenon. When the gate is negatively biased, NBTI as a major aging mechanism affects PMOS transistors [2], [3]. NBTI inducts positive charge accumulation at the oxide-substrate interface and in the oxide layer, and hence, it increases the threshold voltage [7], [9], [10], [19]. As a result, the circuit-level delay increases, and the frequency decreases, leading to degrading the reliability. The threshold voltage presents the recovery on the removal part of the stress [2]. Aging estimation exploits the reactiondiffusion (R-D) based model which is shown in [10] to compute the threshold voltage degradation such that multiple cycles of stress and recovery are considered [3]. The constants, variables, and their values are defined in [1], [10]. We compute the core frequency at time t by considering changing the threshold voltage (ΔV th ) and the PV-led initial safe operating frequency f 0 [1], [3]:
div.formula: f (t) = f 0 × 1 - ΔV th V dd -V th (1)
div.p: where ΔV th is considered according to the following equation [1], [3]:
div.formula: ΔV th = k.A(T, V DD ).Y n .t n (2)
div.p: where Y indicates the amount of stress, K is a fitting parameter, t is the amount of elapsed time, and n depends on diffusing species, A depends on environmental factors such as temperature and supply voltage and is obtained from the following equation [1], [3]:
div.formula: A(T, V dd ) = exp -E 0 K B T .e B.V dd t ox .K B T (3)
div.p: where t ox is the effect of oxide thickness, K B is the Boltzmann constant, E 0 = 0.189eV is the electric field across the channel, and B = 0.075nm/V is the Poisson parameter for trap distribution [1], [2].

div.head: C. Reliability Model
div.p: High reliability is a major design objective in most of safetycritical systems and is subject to different types of faults [18]. The faults may occur due to transient and permanent faults at runtime, e.g., cosmic ray radiations, electromagnetic interference, hardware defects, etc. [20]- [22]. In this paper, transient faults are detected and tolerated because the transient faults occur more frequently than permanent faults with a ratio of 100:1 or higher [23], [24]. Transient faults are modeled as a "Poisson" distribution [6], [21], [22], [25]. The fault rate is based on a function of the normalized frequency or voltage changes [6], [21], [22], [25]. In our ATLAS model, the transient fault rate is computed as [20], [21]:

where λ 0 is the transient fault rate at f max and d determines the sensitivity of the system to frequency scaling [6]. The failure rate can be represented by λ(f ) × F V I. Note that the Function Vulnerability Index (F V I) is the task's susceptibility to failure due to hardware-level transient faults at the instruction-level [6]. Since aging has a negative effect on the frequency of the cores, the reliability of the tasks degrades by decreasing the frequency [2]. Therefore, the reliability of a task at time t can be written as:
div.formula: R(T i , t) = e -λ(f )×F V I× w f (t) (5)
div.p: where w is the number of required clock cycles for executing the task, and f (t) represents the operating frequency of the designated core at time t. Since the operating frequency of the cores depends on aging, we should find it for reliability according to Eq. 1. Therefore, the reliability of a task on a processing core can be rewritten as:
div.formula: R(T i , t) = e -λ(f (t))×F V I× w f (t) (6)
div.p: When r identical copies of a task T i are executed, the reliability of the task is computed based on the probability of having at least one successful execution of them and is calculated as:
div.formula: R rep (T i , r, t) = 1 - r i=1 (1 -R(T i , t)) (7)
div.p: Generally, the total reliability of the system can be computed as:
div.formula: R total (t) = n i=1 R rep (T i , r, t)(8)
div.p: In this paper, if during executing a job, no fault has been detected, its results are considered as the correct output for the system, and its corresponding replica job(s) is dropped (canceled). However, when a fault happens, the faulty job is disclaimed. Then, we continue with its replica job(s) and consider the results of the correct replica job(s) as the perfect results. Note that the checking test or acceptance test ran at job completion times because the occurrence of a fault is indeterminate and running the mentioned test for each time slot of jobs incurs significant overhead (i.e., the time and power overhead). Therefore, when the main job finishes successfully, the corresponding replica job(s) can be dropped or canceled. To do this, a low-overhead fault detection method is exploited. Actually, our ATLAS technique requires a low-cost hardware checker (e.g., Argus [26] which is a low-overhead, comprehensive, low-power, low-cost, and highaccuracy fault detection hardware checker. Argus prepares "run-time checking of control flow, computation, data flow, and memory invariants" [26] which is adequate for detecting soft errors [26]. In our ATLAS method, if no fault has been detected during the execution of a job or task by Argus, its results are supplied to the system and its other replica tasks are dropped or canceled. However, when a fault occurs, the faulty job or task is ignored and its replica job or task is considered, and then the results of the replica job or task are applied to the system as the correct results.

div.head: III. PROBLEM DEFINITION
div.p: In this paper, a multicore system with m cores that executes a set of n periodic hard real-time tasks is considered. The problem is how to find the mapping and scheduling of the tasks (i.e., the start time s ij and the finish time f ij of all original and replica jobs), and the v/f level of each job to satisfy both reliability target and thermal constraint. In this formulation, v is the number of available v/f levels for each core. The task mapping and v/f level assignments are shown in the matrix X ∈ {0, 1} n×m×v . The task i is mapped to the core k and is executed under the v/f level l if and only if X ikl = 1. We formulate the above-mentioned problem in the following.

1) Reliability Target: The total reliability of each task should be equal to or greater than the reliability target R target . Therefore, in order to determine the required number of replicas for each task at time t, there is a minimum number of replicas required to satisfy the task-level reliability target. Based on Eq. 7, the optimal number of replicas needed to satisfy the task-level reliability target is determined.
div.formula: R rep (T i , r, t) = 1 - r i=1 (1 -R(T i , t)) ≥ R target (9)
div.p: 2) Task-to-Core Assignment Constraint: In order to map the task to the processing cores, each task should just be assigned to a designated processing core. ∀i, l :
div.formula: k X ikl = 1 (10)
div.p: 3) Peak Power Constraint at each time slot t: The maximum power consumption of each processing core at each time slot t should be less than TSP.
div.formula: ∀k : P ower C(k) ≤ P T SP,k , at each time t (11)
div.p: 4) Task timing Constraints: The start time and the finish time for the job j of task i on the core k should meet the task order constraint.
div.formula: ∀i, j : (j -1)×d i ≤ s ij +wc ij +intre. ij ≤ f ij ≤ j ×d i (12)
div.p: where intre. ij is the time overhead of preemption.

div.head: 5) Voltage and Frequency Level Constraint:
div.p: In order to set a voltage and frequency level for tasks, we should consider that each task can only be executed under a single v/f level. ∀i, k :
div.formula: l X ikl ≤ 1 (13)
div.p: 6) Utilization Constraint: The total utilization of the system should be less than the number of cores, and the sum of all tasks' utilization mapped on each processing core k should be less than 1.
div.formula: U tot ≤ m (14) ∀k, l : i X kl U i ≤ 1(15)
div.p: The aforementioned problem of scheduling and mapping a set of hard real-time periodic tasks on a multicore platform is an NP-hard problem [6], [18], [25]. Therefore, finding an optimal mapping and scheduling solution will have exponentialtime complexity. In this paper, to solve the problem, we propose an aging-aware mapping and scheduling heuristic method under the aforementioned constraints.

div.head: IV. AGING-AWARE MAPPING AND SCHEDULING METHOD
div.p: In this paper, we aim to optimally determine the required number of replicas to satisfy the task-level reliability target according to Eq. 9 under aging effects. To do this, an agingaware task replication method is proposed to solve the problem of satisfying a desired reliability target for a set of periodic hard real-time tasks running on a safety-critical multicore system. To meet the temperature constraint, the proposed method selects at design time the v/f level of each task to meet the Thermal Safe Power (TSP) constraint. The power consumption of the cores below TSP ensures that thermal violations are avoided. Then, the proposed method replicates the tasks such that the reliability target is satisfied. To decelerate aging mechanisms, our method attempts to reduce the temperature while mapping the tasks. In particular, at each hyperperiod, we sort the tasks based on the peak power consumption in ascending order. Then, the original tasks are mapped to the cores with the lowest temperature policy in which a core with the minimum value of temperature on the chip is selected to execute the task, and then the temperature of all cores is updated. For mapping the replica tasks, we map them to the cores based on the lowest temperature policy. After mapping the tasks to the cores, the tasks and their replicas are scheduled based on the partitioned EDF scheduling policy. At runtime, after each job finishes successfully, the execution of the remaining parts of its other corresponding replica job(s) are canceled to further reduce the power consumption because only at most one successful replica of each job is needed. The overview of this process is shown in Fig. 5. We should mention that all of the techniques used for mapping and scheduling are offline and their overhead can be ignored but some simple operations such as dropping the tasks and some simple computations done in runtime. However, in the offline phase, we decide about dropping the tasks and applying the DVFS technique. Indeed, we just extract some instructions from memory to apply them and the overheads are negligible. Moreover, the time overhead of de/charging the load capacitances is considered in the worstcase execution of the tasks.

div.head: A. Algorithm Discussion
div.p: To solve the aforementioned problem, a mapping and scheduling method for safety-critical systems is proposed to satisfy the timing, reliability, and temperature constraints, considering aging effects. Algorithm 1 shows the pseudocode of our ATLAS method. This algorithm gets the ready tasks with their worst-case execution time and deadlines, the peak power consumption of the tasks, the set of free cores, the available v/f levels, the task-level reliability target, and the core-level power constraint, i.e., TSP.

In line 1, the algorithm determines the time point of the system in which a new hyperperiod is released. In line 2, the frequency of the cores under aging effects based on Eq. 1 is determined. In lines 3-10, for each task Ti, the algorithm is repeated to set the v/f of the task such that the core-level power constraint (TSP) is met. It also determines the number of its replicas to satisfy the task-level reliability target. In particular, in line 4, the algorithm updates the peak power consumption of the task Ti because when the frequency of the cores reduces, the peak power consumption of the task Ti will be reduced. To meet the core-level power constraint (TSP), the algorithm selects an appropriate v/f level for each task in line 5. When the v/f level of each task is specified, the algorithm updates the utilization of each task because the worst-case execution time of the tasks changes according to their frequency levels. In order to satisfy the task-level reliability target, the algorithm adds replicas one by one until the reliability target is satisfied (lines 6-9). For mapping the original and replica tasks, the algorithm sorts them based on their peak power consumption in ascending order, and puts the sorted original and replica tasks into two queues, respectively, i.e., ϕ 1 and ϕ 2 (lines 12-13). In lines 14-24, the algorithm iterates until all original tasks are mapped to the cores. To do this, the algorithm selects the original tasks from the queue ϕ 1 , and then, it maps the selected task to a core with the lowest temperature such that the utilization of the selected core after mapping the selected task is less or equal to 1. Note, every time when an event happens we update the temperature of the cores. The algorithm updates the utilization of the selected core in line 18. To map the replica tasks, in lines 25-35, the algorithm iterates until all replica tasks are mapped to the cores. The algorithm selects the replica tasks from the queue ϕ 2 , and then, it maps the selected task to a core with the lowest temperature such that the utilization of the selected core after mapping the selected replica task is less or equal to 1. After mapping the tasks and replicas, the algorithm schedules them on the cores according to the Earliest-Deadline-First policy. To do this, in line 36, the algorithm calculates the hyperperiod based on the periods of the tasks. Then, the algorithm initializes a schedule S i for each core C i to Null. In lines 38-40, the algorithm calls the EDF function to schedule the tasks and their replicas on each core.

The EDF function is based on the earliest deadline first policy. In this function, when a job J ij arrives, the job is added to the ready queue. When a job J ij is released, if the designated core C i is idle, the job J ij is executed. However, if the core is executing another job, the priorities are considered according to the EDF policy. If preemption happens, the executing job J mn is preempted, and the core executes the current released job J ij . This process is applied to all jobs of all tasks on all cores.

It is worthy to mention that in the offline phase (design time), our ATLAS method guarantees that the deadline, power Algorithm 1: Aging-Aware Mapping and Scheduling Algorithm Input: Ready tasks ϕ = {T 1 , T 2 , . . . , T n } with the worstcase execution time wc i and their deadlines d i (periods), The peak power consumption of the tasks (T 1 .P ow, . . . , T n .P ow), the set of free cores C = {C 1 , C 2 , . . . , C m }, available v/f levels, the task-level reliability target R target , the core-level power constraint, i.e. TSP. Output: Task mapping and scheduling for each hyperperiod.

1: Determine the time point of the system at each hyperperiod; 2: Determine the freq. reduction of cores due to aging; //based on Eq. 1 S i .EDF(C i .ϕ) 40: end for constraints, and reliability targets are met and also reduces the aging effects. To do this, our proposed algorithm determined the required number of replicas for each task and then maps and schedules them so that the mentioned constraints are satisfied. Moreover, in some situations, our scheduler schedules the main and replica tasks in parallel but we will try to reduce the overlap between them because if a task is not faulty, the replica tasks can be dropped and we can save more power/energy consumption, time, and thermal.

At runtime, some jobs of the replica tasks that corresponding main jobs are executed successfully is canceled. For detecting the faults, our task replication method requires a fault detection method. To do this, the cores employ a low-cost and low-power checker like Argus [26]. If, during the execution of the main job, the fault has not been detected, its result is applied to the system, and its corresponding replica job(s) are dropped. Note that the frequency of the processing cores is determined after canceling each task and is updated at each hyperperiod to consider aging effects. Otherwise, when a fault occurs, our proposed method does not apply the result of the faulty job and continues with its replica job(s) and applies the results of the replica job(s). Then, the required number of replicas for each task is updated based on the updated frequency of the cores. Now, the algorithm remaps the tasks and their replicas to the cores according to the offline mapping policy (explained in lines 14-35 of Algorithm 1). Finally, the algorithm re-schedules the main and replica jobs of the tasks (explained in lines 36-40 of Algorithm 1). Note that when some jobs are dropped, in the next hyperperiods, due to the updated frequency of the cores, the required number of replicas may reduce, and hence, the algorithm needs to remap and reschedule the tasks.

div.head: B. Demand Bound Function Analysis
div.p: According to the EDF policy for the presented task set, the analysis of a set of periodic hard real-time tasks with deadlines equal to periods (our presented task model) is performed using the processor demand criterion [27], [28]. This mentioned mechanism had been proposed for interrupt handling costs under the EDF scheduling policy. Note that this test when is used that the deadlines are not equal to periods. Otherwise, the utilization-based analysis should be used, i.e., the total utilization should be less than or equal to 1.

In general, the processing core k demand of a periodic task T i in an time interval [t 1 , t 2 ] is the amount of processing time g k , i (t 1 , t 2 ) requested by the jobs of T i activated in [t 1 , t 2 ] that should be completed in the mentioned time interval [t 1 , t 2 ]. g k , i (t 1 , t 2 ) can be written as:
div.formula: g k,i (t 1 , t 2 ) = rij ≥t1,dij ≤t2 wc i (16
div.p: For the system, the processing core demand in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ] is given by:
div.formula: g k (t 1 , t 2 ) = i∈ck g k,i (t 1 , t 2 )(17)
div.p: Note that the voltage and frequency setting of the tasks are determined before the mapping and scheduling and we just add them to the system to execute based on the EDF scheduling policy. Therefore, we have two utilization for each task: (1) initial task utilization that is user-defined and the input of the system; (2) the main utilization of the task after DVFS setting that is according to meeting the TSP constraint. In order to guarantee the feasibility of the task set, we consider the second utilization of the task that is after setting the voltage and frequency of the tasks for meeting TSP. The feasibility of a task set on the whole of the system is guaranteed if and only if in any interval of time the system demand does not exceed the available time on all the cores; that is, if and only if:
The number of jobs of task T i that should be considered in the time interval [t 1 , t 2 ] can be expressed as:
div.formula: μ i (t 1 , t 2 ) = max{0, t 2 + T i -D i T i - t 1 T i }(19)

V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, our ATLAS method with state-of-the-art methods is compared in terms of reliability, temperature, feasibility (as the percentage of meeting both timing and temperature constraints), and schedulability (as the percentage of satisfying timing constraints) is evaluated. The tool flow of our evaluations is represented in Fig. 6. In our experiments, an ARM processor is considered which is widely exploited in many real-time embedded systems [8]. Moreover, our simulations are conducted on gem5 [14] and McPAT [15] for 14 nm with out-of-order Cortex-A15 cores. Note that the modified McPAT is considered to support 14nm [29]. These tools, i.e., gem5 and McPAT, determine system-level parameters such as the power/energy consumption, the worstcase execution time, and the reliability of the tasks. The details of architecture configurations are shown in Table II. Moreover, we exploit QUILT [30] that generates the floorplan of the platform based on the results of McPAT. For extracting the RC-thermal model of the platform, which is necessary to compute TSP for each processing core [13], HotSpot [16] is exploited. Our simulations are running with various real-time task sets, including real-life real-time embedded applications of MiBench Benchmark [11] running on a target homogeneous multicore platform with a different number of cores, e.g., 4, 9, and 16 cores. To generate task sets, a different number of tasks is selected from the MiBench Benchmark based on different utilizations. Then, a system-level scheduler is developed to simulate different execution scenarios. Finally, TSP is exploited to compute the core-level power constraints. In our evaluations, we compare our ATLAS method with state-of-the-art power and reliability co-management techniques. The comparison schemes are:
• EM [18]: Haque et al. [18] have presented an energyaware task replication technique for multicore real-time embedded systems.

• PPARM [6]: Ansari et al. in [6] have presented a peakpower-aware reliability management technique. This technique replicates different versions of each task (code version programming) to meet the task-level reliability target while meeting TSP [6].

• ReMap [31]: The authors in this work have proposed a method for the problem of satisfying a desired reliability target by considering the chip TDP constraint. We compared our ATLAS method with the three mentioned schemes (EM, PPARM, ReMap) for the realistic execution scenario when the system consumes real power and temperature.

In order to inject the faults, we have considered that transient faults occur with a Poisson process [18], [31]. To do this, using Eq. 4 under the parameters λ 0 = 10 -6 f aults/μs and d = 2 [18], [31], the fault rate is generated. In our evaluations, a fault vector is generated for each processing core that determines at which times faults occur. According to the generated fault vectors, we decide which jobs or tasks become faulty at runtime.

In our evaluation, we compare the feasibility, schedulability, reliability, and maximum temperature of the proposed method with state-of-the-art methods. To analyze the ATLAS method for each system configuration, we exploit several task sets simulated 100 times with different input parameters and the average results are reported.

div.head: A. Evaluating feasibility and schedulability in the design time
div.p: In this subsection, the feasibility and schedulability are analyzed in the design time. Note that in the context of the paper, feasibility is the percentage of meeting both timing and temperature constraints. Also, schedulability is just the percentage of meeting timing constraints. In Fig. 7, we reported our comparison with three state-of-the-art methods in terms of feasibility in the design time for different per-core utilizations. The results of this figure are reported from the offline part of our ATLAS method that considers the worstcase scenario where all main and replica tasks will be executed completely. Because we should guarantee that both timing and temperature constraints are met in the design time. As seen in Fig. 7, the feasibility of our ATLAS method is higher than two state-of-the-art methods, i.e., ReMap and EM. This is because ReMap and EM have not considered the temperature constraint in their method. However, PPARM has a similar rate of feasibility to our ATLAS method because PPARM meets the TSP and timing constraints simultaneously. It should be noted that PPARM has not considered the effect of aging on reliability, and in Fig. 9, we show that the reliability of the PPARM method decreases at different years. The feasibility results show that our ATLAS method meets the timing and temperature constraints on average by 63.2% while the stateof-the-art methods meet the mentioned constraints on average by 41.5%. Therefore, our ATLAS method is more efficient than other state-of-the-art techniques for satisfying the timing and temperature constraints simultaneously in safety-critical multicore systems. Fig. 8 shows the schedulability ratio of different methods in the design time for different per-core utilizations. This figure shows that the schedulability of our ATLAS method is on average 76.6% while the other methods meet the deadlines on average by 60.5%.

div.head: B. Evaluating reliability at runtime
div.p: Fig. 9 reports the reliability of applications for our ATLAS method and the state-of-the-art methods. Note that tasks are selected from the level of B in the DO-178B standard [37]. Regarding the selected level, the proper number of replicas will be selected at each hyperperiod for our ATLAS method. Note that other methods determine the number of replicas in the design time, and their numbers are fixed. Obviously, the reliability of EM, PPARM, and ReMap degrades because they did not update the number of replicas after passing years.

div.head: C. Evaluating the maximum temperature at runtime
div.p: In this subsection, in order to have a fair comparison, we assume that EM, PPARM, and ReMap similar to our ATLAS method, update the number of replicas based on our proposed aging-aware reliability formulas. Fig. 10 shows that in order to satisfy different reliability targets, we should add more replicas and also update the number of replicas according to the aging-aware reliability at different years. As shown in Fig. 10, at the start time of the system, all the methods meet the temperature constraint, while after passing years, the stateof-the-art methods violate the temperature constraint, but our proposed method meets it.

div.head: VI. RELATED WORK
div.p: Task replication technique on multicore safety-critical systems relies on mapping and scheduling the different number of replicas of tasks on different processing cores. The main key of the task replication technique is to guarantee that at most one of the replicas is needed to be executed at run time, and at least one copy of each task will be completed before the hard timing constraint in the situation of fault occurrence. Wang et al. [32] have improved the reliability of tasks through a task replication mechanism. They have presented a method that mathematically computes the number of replica tasks. Note that the goal in [32] is to maximize the total performance index, which is a performance-aware reliability computation factor. The authors in [33] have proposed a method for integrating the different number of tasks into the scheduling phase of their proposed algorithms in hard real-time systems.

Chen et al. [34] have considered the task replication method for periodic hard real-time tasks in homogeneous multiprocessor systems. Each replica of a periodic hard real-time task is scheduled and executed on different K processors. The objective function of [34] is to optimize the maximum utilization for a system that has a specified number of processing components. To do this, they have presented a 2-approximation ratio and a polynomial-time approximation method through a greedy algorithm. The authors in [35] have considered only two replicas for each task and mapped tasks to a heterogeneous platform such that timing constraints are met and one permanent fault can be tolerated. Litke et al. [36] have presented an efficient task replication scheme that exploits the Weibull reliability formula for the Grid environment to determine the number of replicas. In [36], the additional workload through the task replication method is managed by a resource management scheme that is based on the knapsack formulation. Their proposed method aims to maximize the utilization and benefit of the Grid infrastructure. The authors in [37] have solved the problem of maximizing the number of successfully assigned tasks to a homogeneous multicore platform such that the real-time constraint and systems-level reliability target are met. Kim et al. [38] have proposed a System-level Architecture for Failure Evasion in Real-time applications (SAFER) to combine adjustable tasklevel redundancy to tolerate transient and permanent faults for embedded real-time systems. To detect both faults, SAFER monitors the situation and information of each task and each core and broadcasts the information. When a fault is detected using their detection method, SAFER changes the structure of the system to keep the functionality of the system. Spasic et al. [39] have presented a polynomial-time method to determine a processing component type for executing each task in a graph-based application such that the throughput is maximized and the energy consumption is reduced. They also determine a replication factor for each task in a graph such that the utilization of each processor is balanced, which enables processors to execute the tasks at lower v/f levels for reducing the total energy consumption. Haque et al. [18] have proposed a reliability-aware energy management method for executing preemptive periodic real-time applications on a multicore realtime system. The authors in [18] have presented a technique to determine the replication and frequency level for each task while minimizing the overall energy of the system. Ansari et al. [6] have proposed a solution for meeting the chip-and core-level power constraints and task-level reliability target by exploiting different versions of each task (code version programming).

The authors in [40] have presented a reliability-aware energy management method that optimizes energy consumption and satisfies the system reliability target through dynamic task replication while meeting timing and power constraints. They have modeled their problem as convex optimization and solved it through existing solvers. Salehi et al. [41] have presented a power-aware reliability management technique for many-core systems. They employ various redundancy types executing on different v/f levels. Safari et al. [22] have proposed a scheme that simultaneously guarantees certification, energy reduction, fault tolerance, and a minimum service level for mixed-criticality multicore embedded systems. They use task replication to not only meet reliability targets but also to improve the QoS of low-criticality tasks in the overrun situation of the system. Their proposed scheme computes the required number of replicas for each high-criticality task and reduces the execution time overlap between the main tasks and their replicas to reduce energy consumption. The goal of [25] is to calculate the level of task replication, frequency level, and core allocation for each task at design time to achieve a desired reliability target while minimizing the overall energy consumption of the system. The authors in [42] have suggested that by scheduling the different number of copies for the tasks on different cores in a multicore system, the probability of successfully completing at least one copy of the tasks increases significantly. Also, they have proved that task replication has some intrinsic features for reliability improvement.

As it is mentioned, none of the previous work in the context of safety-critical systems considered the aging-aware task replication method such that the reliability, timing, and temperature constraint are met. The purpose of this work is to propose a method that satisfies timing, reliability, and temperature constraints under aging effects.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we have proposed an aging-aware task replication method that solves the problem of satisfying a desired reliability target for a set of periodic hard real-time tasks executing on a multicore embedded system under aging effects. Since the reliability of the tasks degrades by decreasing the frequency of the cores due to aging, the proposed method satisfies the reliability target of the tasks by adding replica tasks at different years. Moreover, in order to meet the temperature constraint of the system, we set the v/f level of each task, and then, we replicate the tasks such that the reliability target is satisfied. In order to meet the timing constraints, we map the tasks and their replicas to the cores according to the lowest temperature policy, such that the utilization of each core is less than 1. After mapping the tasks to the cores, we schedule the tasks and their replicas based on the partitioned EDF scheduling policy. Compared to the existing state-of-the-art techniques, experimental results for hard real-time applications on different configurations of multicore systems demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of our proposed method.
